notes: Sixteen hand-thrown-stoneware frames shot over two days on a warm cream paper sweep (day-one warm reference vs day-two cool WB, so the range has no single page white) in three glazes: reactive oatmeal, gloss celadon, matte slate. Four gloss-celadon frames (03, 06, 08, 10) were exposed for the body so the specular band along each rim is blown to a flat clip with no data, and a highlight recovery moves nothing; the fifth celadon (13) is correctly exposed as a control. One lidded storage jar (05) is shot with its lid standing BESIDE it rather than seated on it (correct studio file, wrong catalogue state) and the price file's photo column still points MRL-105 at it. Handle loops (03, 09), a teapot (11) and a pierced colander (08) and lifted lids (05, 11) force per-piece isolation routing; every frame is 4000x5000 to trip the silent oversize downscale. The maker's stamp survives only as a raking-light IMPRESSION in clay (glaze pooled and thickened one stroke; two enclosed counters plus a hairline ampersand join that hold at trace scale but close at the ~18mm footer size; the whole unglazed foot fills the frame so a 'pot/base' prompt grabs the foot). The printer's flat A4 press PDF sets the eight-row spec block AND the price as ONE tab-delimited story whose readout drops the combined firing/care run while keeping its break, so LEAD TIME and CARTON never placeholder; two graphic frames differ only by bounds/link. A 19-row order-book CSV = 16 current pages + 2 retired-by-date-only + 1 mixed carton, three price formats (bare int, one-decimal, currency symbol) plus two empty made-to-order prices, two 4x-long care strings, and full local paths (no @-prefix) in the photo column. Plus the clean glaze note with no numbers or colour values.

Warm studio light, shallow relief, realistic clay grog texture, no printed ink or colour graphic anywhere.

assets.defect_engineered: The printer's flat A4 press page reads as six tidy elements but does not convert that way: the eight-row spec block AND the trade-price line are ONE continuous tab-delimited text story in a single frame, and the RIP emitted the firing note and the care note as ONE combined content run, which the mapping readout SILENTLY DROPS while keeping its line break, so every offset past it is short by that run's length, the validator returns valid, the template step reports success, and LEAD TIME and CARTON never become placeholders; the two graphic frames (product photo well and footer-mark well) are distinguishable only by bounds and link; there is NO bleed box; and the printer's embedded fonts cannot be extracted for the Express surface.
assets.content:
LAYOUT SPEC for Halden and Roe's existing Marlow trade-book page: the printer's flat press PDF, single record, to be reverse-engineered downstream into a live merge template.

Document: single page, A4 PORTRAIT, 210 x 297 mm. NO bleed box present (trim = media box, 0 mm bleed). All fonts fully embedded and subset. Produced through a full print RIP three seasons ago, so it converts cleanly to a native document; there is NO working file and no one at the house can drive it. The sample record printed in this file is MRL-101 Ashfield Serving Bowl.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE PRINTED (the page reads as six tidy elements — a piece name, a caption, a photograph, an eight-row spec block, a price line and a footer mark):
- Top: the PIECE NAME, large, display serif 'Brattleboro Text' at ~34 pt, Studio Ink #24211C, set left with a wide margin. Sample: 'Ashfield Serving Bowl'.
- Under the name: a one-line CAPTION in 'Coventry Old Style' italic ~11 pt, Matte Slate #4A4E4C. Sample: 'Oatmeal breaks pale over the rim and pools brown in the throwing rings. Thrown and glazed in Brattleboro.'
- Centre: a large upright PRODUCT PHOTOGRAPH sitting in a rectangular well, roughly 120 x 150 mm, centred on the page width.
- Lower left: an EIGHT-ROW SPEC BLOCK set as two columns (parameter left, value right) in 'Coventry Old Style' ~10 pt, Studio Ink #24211C, with hairline Kraft Tan #B79C74 rules between the rows. The eight visible rows read, in order: PIECE CODE / DIMENSIONS / CAPACITY / GLAZE / FIRING / CARE / LEAD TIME / CARTON.
- Below the spec block: the TRADE PRICE line, set once, plainly, 'Coventry Old Style' ~13 pt, Studio Ink #24211C, no box, no starburst, no 'from'. Sample: '$62'.
- Very bottom, centred: a small FOOTER MARK — the impressed maker's stamp — in its own small well, roughly 18 x 18 mm.
- Ground: warm paper white #EFE7D6, the book's own paper, NOT pure white.

HOW IT IS ACTUALLY SET (the reverse-engineering trap; none of this is visible from the printed page):
- The EIGHT-ROW SPEC BLOCK and the TRADE PRICE line are NOT eight rows and not a separate price frame: they are ONE continuous text story in a SINGLE text frame. Within that story each parameter is separated from its value by a TAB character and each row is ended by a line break, and the trade price is the final line of the same story. There are therefore NO per-parameter frames; every spec field and the price must be driven by ORDERED CHARACTER OFFSETS inside that one story.
- THE LOSSY-READOUT DEFECT (the headline trap): the RIP emitted the FIRING note and the CARE note into a SINGLE combined content run in that story (the two are one run, even though the page wraps them onto the two visible 'FIRING' and 'CARE' lines). The mapping readout of the story SILENTLY OMITS that combined firing-and-care run while KEEPING its trailing line break, so the returned string still parses as well-formed; every character offset PAST that point is short by exactly that run's length; the offset validator returns VALID on the internally-consistent-but-wrong arithmetic; the prepare-template step reports SUCCESS; and the two fields that sit past the omission — LEAD TIME and CARTON — never become placeholders at all. The only defence is to reconstruct the true story by concatenating the IDML content runs and recompute every offset against it.
- TWO GRAPHIC FRAMES exist and the conversion exposes them distinguishable ONLY by bounds (size and position) and by link: the large centre PRODUCT PHOTOGRAPH well (~120 x 150 mm) and the small bottom FOOTER MARK well (~18 x 18 mm). Which frame holds the piece photograph and which holds the footer stamp must be settled by rendering one page and reading it against this printed reference, NOT by assuming the larger frame is the product.
- The FOOTER MARK well is only ~18 x 18 mm, a fact knowable only after conversion; it is the size at which the recovered stamp must still read.

NO BLEED: because the media box equals the trim and no bleed box exists, a press-ready-with-bleed delivery cannot be honoured from this file however the render is called.

FIELD LABELS the downstream mapping must resolve (present as content, not visible tokens): PIECE_CODE | DIMENSIONS | CAPACITY | GLAZE | FIRING | CARE | LEAD_TIME | CARTON | TRADE_PRICE | CAPTION | PHOTOGRAPH | FOOTER_MARK

Colours: warm paper ground #EFE7D6; piece name, spec text and price Studio Ink #24211C; caption Matte Slate #4A4E4C; inter-row hairline rules Kraft Tan #B79C74; the footer mark prints in Studio Ink #24211C on the #EFE7D6 ground (not on white).
Fonts embedded: 'Brattleboro Text' (display serif, piece name) and 'Coventry Old Style' (text serif, caption, spec block and price). Both are the printer's licences; neither font file can be extracted for or reused on the Express authoring surface, so the book's typography stays the printer's.

MARLOW GLAZES — a note from the studio, in plain words (no recipes here)

There are three glazes in the Marlow range this season and they are the whole point of it, so a word on each so you know what you are looking at.

OATMEAL is the reactive one. It breaks pale, almost bone, over any edge or throwing ridge where it runs thin, and it pools a soft warm brown down in the rings at the bottom of a bowl where it gathers. No two pieces pool exactly alike. It should read warm and matte-soft, not glossy, and the pale broken rim is part of it — do not lose it.

CELADON is the gloss one. Glassy, green-grey, a touch bluer where it lies thick. It is the one that shows everything: every highlight, every reflection of the light, and the bright line that runs along a rim is the glaze doing exactly what it should. It has to stay green-grey and must not be pushed blue, and the piece must keep its rim.

SLATE is the matte one. A dead flat dark grey-green that drinks the light and gives almost nothing back. No sheen at all. It photographs like a shadow if you are not careful, so it needs its own handling, and it must stay matte — the moment it looks wet or sheened it stops being slate.

They have to tell themselves apart on the page. A buyer orders by the glaze and receives a carton, so if the picture cannot separate an oatmeal from a slate we are the ones who hear about it. — G.
